query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-depositing a thin titanium layer on the tungsten phase so that, during subsequent high‐temperature and irradiation processing, an in situ TiC interlayer forms at the W/Cu interfaces, thereby suppressing phase separation and interfacial void formation.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite containing discrete tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that exhibits phase separation and void formation at the interfaces under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a thin Ti coating (via physical vapor deposition or similar technique) on the tungsten surfaces prior to composite consolidation and heat treatment.
generation.conditions: Processing and service conditions relevant to plasma-facing W components joined to Cu-based cooling structures, including high heat flux and irradiative environments (temperatures and irradiation doses typical for fusion reactor divertor/joint regions).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent, thin TiC interlayer at the W/Cu interface.
generation.mechanism: During heat treatment, the Ti coating reacts with residual carbon (or from the environment) to form TiC. This in situ TiC layer acts as a robust diffusion barrier to limit interdiffusion and phase separation while filling voids and enhancing interfacial bonding, thereby lowering interfacial thermal resistance and improving thermal conductivity under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated composites, the intervention should yield a composite with fewer interfacial voids, reduced phase separation, and improved thermal conductivity, ensuring better joint performance under heat‐transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated W–Cu composite that, under similar processing and service conditions, exhibits phase separation, interfacial voids, and consequently, inferior thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the Ti coating is expected within the operational temperature range and irradiation flux relevant to fusion reactor joints; however, its performance may be limited if temperatures or irradiation doses exceed those typically encountered in current designs.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimum thickness of the titanium layer and the kinetics of TiC formation (especially under irradiation) need further experimental tuning. Also, potential secondary effects of the Ti or TiC phase on mechanical properties under cyclic loading remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite specimens: one set with a pre-deposited thin Ti layer on the tungsten phase and a control set without the coating. Process both sets under identical heat-treatment schedules and subject them to simulated irradiation conditions representative of plasma-facing joint environments.
measurements: High-resolution SEM/TEM to assess interfacial microstructure (voids and phase separation)
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Evaluation of interfacial bonding strength and irradiation-induced microstructural changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-coated specimens do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity and thermal conductivity relative to the control, or if they exhibit adverse microstructural or mechanical effects under irradiation, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The W-based composite having uniformly distributed TiC within the grains and along the grain boundaries can withstand heat flux as high as 200 MW/m2, which is nearly 100% higher than the flux sustained by pure W. An increase in the amount of the evenly distributed TiC in the W matrix (inside the grains and along the boundaries) also increases the hardness creep strength and modulus of elasticity, , . The presence of TiC in the grains and on the grain boundaries also favors fusion applications, as it increases the recrystallization temperature and irradiation resistance. TiC does not have a significant effect on the deuterium retention behavior of W-based materials, . The dispersion of carbides in the grain boundaries of W leads to grain boundary strengthening and provides some resistance to grain boundary migration at elevated temperatures. Therefore, TiC is considered to be beneficial in high-temperature and plasma-facing alloys. The volume fraction of TiC in the xWs samples determined by analyzing the SEM images was found to vary from 1.1 to 8.5% (Table S3).
